When evaluating the performance of a locally hosted large language model, it is essential to move beyond simple latency numbers and understand the underlying throughput metrics that dictate real-world usability. Throughput, measured in tokens per second, provides a more granular view of how efficiently a system processes requests, but interpreting these numbers requires careful consideration of several variables that can skew results if not properly accounted for. The two primary throughput metrics to track are prompt throughput and generation throughput. Prompt throughput refers to the rate at which the model processes the input tokens, essentially the speed of the attention mechanism as it reads the context. Generation throughput, on the other hand, measures the speed at which the model produces output tokens one by one. These two metrics often differ significantly, especially when dealing with long contexts or small batch sizes, and understanding their relationship is crucial for diagnosing performance bottlenecks.

One of the most common pitfalls in benchmarking is ignoring the effects of batching. When a single request is processed, the overhead of launching the inference kernel and managing memory can dominate the actual computation time, leading to artificially low throughput numbers. By sending multiple requests simultaneously, you can amortize this overhead across many tokens, resulting in higher throughput. However, batching also introduces its own complexities. If the batch size is too large, memory constraints may force the system to swap data between GPU and CPU, drastically reducing performance. Conversely, if the batch size is too small, the GPU may not be fully utilized, leaving computational resources idle. Therefore, it is important to test a range of batch sizes to find the sweet spot that maximizes throughput for your specific hardware configuration.

Context length is another critical factor that influences throughput. As the length of the input context increases, the computational cost of the attention mechanism grows quadratically with respect to the sequence length. This means that processing a prompt with ten thousand tokens will take significantly longer than processing a prompt with one thousand tokens, even if the output length is the same. Additionally, longer contexts require more memory to store the key-value pairs for the attention heads, which can lead to memory pressure and potential swapping. When measuring throughput, it is important to report the context length alongside the throughput numbers, as a model that performs well with short prompts may struggle with longer ones. Some models are optimized for long contexts using techniques like flash attention or sliding window attention, which can mitigate the quadratic scaling issue, but these optimizations come with their own trade-offs in terms of accuracy and memory usage.

Warm cache effects are also a significant consideration when interpreting throughput measurements. When a model is first loaded into memory, the initial requests may be slower due to the time required to load the model weights and initialize the computation graph. Subsequent requests, however, benefit from the model being already in memory, leading to faster response times. This effect is particularly pronounced when switching between different models or when the system has been idle for a period of time. To obtain accurate throughput measurements, it is important to warm up the model by running a few dummy requests before starting the benchmark. This ensures that the model is fully loaded and that the measurements reflect the steady-state performance rather than the initial loading overhead.

Another common source of misleading data is the use of very short outputs. When the output length is very small, the generation throughput can appear artificially high because the overhead of launching the inference kernel is spread over only a few tokens. This can give the impression that the model is extremely fast, but it does not reflect the true performance for typical use cases where outputs are longer. To get a more accurate picture of generation throughput, it is important to use output lengths that are representative of real-world usage, such as a few hundred tokens. Additionally, it is important to consider the distribution of output lengths, as some models may have variable generation speeds depending on the complexity of the task.

Comparing CPU-only, GPU-only, and hybrid runs requires a nuanced understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each configuration. CPU-only runs are generally slower than GPU runs, but they can be more cost-effective and accessible for users who do not have a dedicated GPU. GPU-only runs offer the best performance, but they require a powerful GPU with sufficient memory to handle the model weights and activations. Hybrid runs, which offload some parts of the computation to the CPU and others to the GPU, can provide a balance between performance and resource utilization. However, hybrid runs can be more complex to configure and may not always provide a significant performance improvement over GPU-only runs, depending on the specific model and hardware configuration. When comparing these configurations, it is important to consider not only the throughput but also the memory usage, power consumption, and overall system stability.

In summary, interpreting local LLM throughput measurements requires a holistic approach that takes into account prompt throughput, generation throughput, batch effects, context length effects, warm cache effects, and the choice of hardware configuration. By carefully controlling these variables and reporting them alongside the throughput numbers, you can obtain a more accurate and meaningful assessment of your model's performance. This will enable you to make informed decisions about how to optimize your setup for your specific use case, whether that involves maximizing throughput for high-volume applications or minimizing latency for interactive applications. Ultimately, the goal is to understand not just how fast your model is, but how it behaves under different conditions, so that you can tailor your deployment strategy to meet the needs of your users.
